content: 1. Patient costs associated with accessing health services should be considered more broadly to ensure equitable access to care. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) has provided updated guidance on facility-based HIV testing services (HTS) and service delivery approaches, including recommendations and good practice statements. 3. WHO's 2017 guidelines on syphilis testing and treatment emphasize the importance of early detection and management of syphilis, particularly in antenatal care (ANC) settings. 4. WHO's 2016 recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience highlight the need for comprehensive care, including testing for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at least once and as early as possible during pregnancy. 5. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) can serve as the first test in HIV testing strategies and algorithms in ANC settings, particularly in high HIV burden areas. 6. In high HIV burden settings, HIV testing should be offered to all populations and integrated into various health services, such as those for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), hepatitis, tuberculosis (TB), immunization, malnutrition, and ANC, to efficiently identify individuals with HIV. 7. In low HIV burden settings, HIV testing should be prioritized for specific groups, including individuals with clinical signs or conditions indicative of HIV, HIV-exposed children, key populations and their partners, and all pregnant women. 8. Community-based HIV testing services, with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment, are recommended in both high and low HIV burden settings, particularly for key populations. 9. HIV self-testing is recommended as an additional approach to HIV testing services, empowering individuals to test themselves in a private and convenient manner. 10. Provider-assisted referral (also known as index testing or assisted partner notification) should be offered to all individuals diagnosed with HIV as part of a voluntary, comprehensive package of testing, care, and prevention services. 11. Social network-based approaches can be used as an HIV testing strategy for key populations, as part of a comprehensive package of care and prevention. 12. Lay providers who are trained and supervised can independently conduct safe and effective HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). 13. Retesting for HIV is recommended for specific groups, such as sexually active individuals in high HIV burden settings, people with ongoing HIV-related risks, and individuals with recent HIV risk exposure. More frequent retesting (every 3–6 months) may be warranted based on individual risk factors. 14. Pregnant women in high HIV burden settings should be retested for HIV in late pregnancy (third trimester) and, if missed, during the postpartum period. Additional testing may be considered in specific high-risk districts or among women with HIV-positive partners who are not virally suppressed. 15. In low HIV burden settings, retesting in late pregnancy or postpartum should focus on women in serodiscordant relationships or those with ongoing HIV risk. 16. WHO recommends that all HIV testing algorithms achieve at least 99% positive predictive value and use a combination of tests with high sensitivity (≥99%) and specificity (≥98%). A three-test strategy is advised as HIV positivity rates fall below 5% in national programs. 17. Rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be offered to all individuals diagnosed with HIV following clinical assessment. This includes same-day initiation where feasible and appropriate. 18. A package of support interventions, such as enhanced linkage with case management, patient tracing, and peer support, should be provided to ensure timely linkage to care for individuals diagnosed with HIV. 19. ART initiation should follow principles of people-centered care, respecting individual dignity and preferences, and empowering individuals to make informed decisions about their care. 20. All individuals newly diagnosed with HIV should be retested to verify their HIV status before starting ART, using the same testing strategy and algorithm as the initial test. 21. Governments are encouraged to revisit age-of-consent policies to uphold adolescents' rights to make decisions about their health and well-being, considering their maturity and understanding. 22. HIV testing services should be routinely offered to all key populations in both community and facility-based settings, with linkage to prevention, treatment, and care. 23. Adolescents from key populations should have access to HIV testing services, with counseling on the benefits and risks of disclosure of their HIV status, and support to make informed decisions about disclosure. 24. In high HIV burden settings, HIV testing services with linkage to care are recommended for all adolescents, while in low HIV burden settings, these services should be accessible to adolescents in concentrated epidemics. 25. Couples and partners should be offered HIV testing services, with updated WHO recommendations emphasizing the importance of partner notification and testing as part of comprehensive care.
